The Khon Kaen Provincial Court has dismissed a royal defamation charge filed against activist Songpol “Yajai” Sonthirak for flashing the three-finger salute at a graduation ceremony in December 2022.
Songpol was charged with royal defamation and violation of the Computer Crimes Act for flashing the three-finger “Hunger Games” salute, a well-known resistance symbol used by activists protesting the 2014 military coup and by students in the 2020 pro-democracy movement, after receiving his degree certificate from Princess Sirindhorn, King Vajiralongkorn’s younger sister, during Khon Kaen University’s graduation ceremony on 20 December 2022. He was also charged for an interview with The Isaan Record and another with a Khon Kaen University student activist group. He was indicted in November 2025.
Khon Kaen University reportedly paused its live broadcast of the graduation ceremony while Songpol and subsequent graduates from the Faculty of Law were receiving their certificates, and did not allow comments on the live broadcast after it resumed.
The complaint against him was filed by Kamon Kitkasiwat, leader of a royalist group in Khon Kaen, who was at the time an MP candidate for the royalist Thai Pakdee Party.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) said today (10 November) that the Khon Kaen Provincial Court has dismissed the charge against Songpol. ECT challenges Supreme Court’s authority to examine Senate candidate qualifications
The Election Commission of Thailand (ECT) has sought a Constitutional Court ruling over the Supreme Court’s authority to examine the qualifications of Senate candidates, amid a controversy over the Senate selection fraud.
The ECT commissioners voted 5-2 to petition the Constitutional Court, asking it to rule whether the Supreme Court had the authority to examine the qualifications of five Senate candidates, two of whom are sitting senators, according to several news outlets.
Three petitions were filed with the Supreme Court by unsuccessful Senate candidates, known as reserve senators. They asked the Court to examine the qualifications of five Senate candidates who had passed the preliminary qualification examination conducted by the ECT. The ECT had judged that these candidates were eligible after an earlier petition filed over their qualifications.
The Supreme Court began reviewing the evidence in October 2025. The Court is expected to conclude the case by the end of this year.
However, the majority of the ECT commissioners claim that by accepting the petitions, the Supreme Court has infringed on the ECT’s authority to oversee the Senate selection process, particularly as these candidates had been officially cleared by the commission.
According to the ECT, the Supreme Court has no authority to initiate on its own the process to revisit the ECT’s final decision.
On 4 November, the ECT filed its petition with the Constitutional Court. The ECT argues that the law narrowly defines the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction, and gives it no authority to initiate investigations into electoral fraud, except in cases referred to the Supreme Court by the ECT itself. Thailand bans new Routledge textbook on contemporary politics, citing national security threats
The Thai police have ordered a ban on the second edition of the Routledge Handbook of Contemporary Thailand, claiming that it contains chapters that could affect national security or cause unrest.
Edited by exiled academic Pavin Chachavalpongpun, the book contains chapters on the Thai military, the monarchy, and the use of the royal defamation law, as well as chapters on popular movements and other social and political issues. Pavin posted on Facebook on Thursday (5 November) that the book was banned for its content about the monarchy.
In a previous post, he wrote that book banning doesn’t work in the age of the internet, since people can buy e-books instead of hard copies. He also wrote that the ban would help promote the book.
Under the 2007 Printing Recordation Act, importing the book for distribution carries a prison sentence of up to three years, or a fine of up to 60,000 baht, or both. The police may also seize and destroy the book.
This is the second time one of Pavin’s publications has been banned in Thailand. In July 2023, the Thai authorities ordered a ban on his book “Rama X: The Thai Monarchy under King Vajiralongkorn” even before it was released.
iLaw noted that the police have banned six books since the Printing Recordation Act came into effect, all of which concerns the monarchy. Other than the two books by Pavin, the list includes:
Thailand’s Crisis and the Fight for Democracy by Giles Ungpakorn A Kingdom in Crisis by Andrew McGregor Marshall The November 2015 issue of the French edition of Marie Claire magazine The article “Thailand: Colossally Popular,” published in The New Age of the Kings: Modern Monarchies in Malaysia and the World

After its release, the animation was criticized by pro-democracy netizens for misinterpreting the events of 1932 and for painting those behind the revolution in a bad light.

The lawsuit stems from a report on 15 March 2024 by Prachatai that, according to the analysis of the Anti-Corruption Organisation of Thailand, the Army had previously commissioned 11 media production projects from the company.

The Appeal Court has dismissed a defamation lawsuit filed by the chicken farm company Thammakaset against three human rights defenders for social media posts about abuse of migrant workers at its farm.
The company filed criminal defamation complaints in 2019 against Angkhana Neelapaijit, Puttanee Kangkun, and Thanaporn Saleephol for sharing and posting on social media in support of migrant workers who reported poor working conditions and other human rights defenders who had been sued by the company.
In August 2023, the South Bangkok Criminal Court dismissed the lawsuit on the grounds that the posts were not about the company but expressed support for other advocates being sued by the company, while a video linked to the posts was found in another case to not be defamatory.

It noted that the posts were not defamatory towards the company and that the business losses that the company claimed were not a direct result of the posts.

Anon is among more than 290 people who have been charged under the royal defamation law since the youth-led protests that began in 2020. He was among the first prominent figures to publicly challenge the longstanding taboo surrounding discussion of the monarchy in Thai https://ow.ly/cc6p5103VJq

Thai authorities should not forcibly return two Uyghur men to China, where they face grave risks of torture and other serious abuses, Human Rights Watch said today (4 November). On October 21, 2026, the authorities transferred them from Bangkok Central Prison to the Bangkok Immigration Detention Center Suan Phlu after they had served most of their seven-year sentence. Thai Foreign Ministry officials told a parliamentary committee that in August the Chinese embassy in Bangkok demanded their return to China.
Under Thai immigration law and regulations, the two Uyghur men will be deported to China unless they object to the deportation and are resettled to a third country. Lawyers representing them told Human Rights Watch that they have already informed Thai authorities that the two do not consent to be sent to China. International Court of Justice to rule on 19 November in Myanmar Genocide case
The International Court of Justice has announced that it will deliver its judgment on November 19, 2026, in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Genocide Convention, Human Rights Watch said today in releasing a question-and-answer document on key issues in the case.
In August 2017, Myanmar’s security forces began a sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, and arson against ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State that forced more than 700,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In November 2019, Gambia filed a case before the International Court of Justice alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya constitute genocide and violate the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. This is not a criminal case against individuals, but a request for a legal determination of Myanmar’s state responsibility for genocide.
“The International Court of Justice’s Myanmar judgment will mark a crucial moment in the Rohingya’s quest for justice,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The ruling will also be a stark reminder that the oppression of the Rohingya is ongoing, and that rights-respecting countries need to act decisively to support them, promote justice for atrocities, and ensure their safe and voluntary return.”
The judgment, which is final with no possibility to appeal, will conclude the proceedings in this case before the court.

On Saturday (31 October), a gathering took place at an overpass on Vibhavadi Road to mark the 20th anniversary of the death of Nuamthong Praiwan, a taxi driver who crashed his taxi into a tank and later took his own life in protest of the 19 September 2006 military coup.
Activists, politicians, and members of the public participated in the gathering, which started at around 12.30 with live music, followed by a Buddhist merit-making ceremony. Flowers were placed around the overpass.
The rapper Elevenfinger also performed at the gathering. Before the event ended, former Red Shirt leader Thida Tavornseth led the participants in making a pledge to push for a new Constitution in line with the result of the 2026 referendum and for the repeal of laws that are relics of military coups.
After the coup, on 30 September 2006, Nuamthong crashed his taxi into a tank parked near the Equestrian Statue of King Chulalongkorn to protest the coup. He was seriously injured..
On 31 October 2006, Nuamthong was found hanging from the overpass in front of the Thairath newspaper office on Vibhavadi Road. He had committed suicide after Akkara Thairoj, a deputy spokesperson for the military junta, expressed scepticism about his intentions by asserting that “nobody’s ideals are so great that they would sacrifice their lives for them.”
Nuamthong’s suicide note says that he voluntarily crashed his taxi and took his own life and that he dies to demand democracy, and that his suicide is also a response to Akkara’s insult. He also wrote that “I hope that in my next life, there shall be no more coups.”
